Pele Yoetz 4:13: And this mitzvah is also incumbent upon the bride's own father and mother, to counsel her before the marriage and afterward, that she act in such-and-such ways, and that she be very careful about the honor of her husband and the honor of her father-in-law and mother-in-law, and her husband's brothers and sisters, and the wives of his brothers and the husbands of his sisters, and all his relatives - for the honor of the LORD, who commanded her to be careful of her husband's honor, and whatever she does to honor her husband's relatives is a service that gives him peace of mind, and she shall find favor in his eyes, and it shall be counted as a mitzvah for her. And it has already been said that there is no need to urge one to be a lover of peace and a pursuer of peace except one from whom peace flees and who has sufficient grounds for quarrel and strife - upon him falls this mitzvah, to be a pursuer of peace for the honor of the Master of peace. But it is necessary to urge the wife not to be light-headed and not to increase conversation, laughter, and levity, and all the more so undue familiarity, with her husband's relatives - rather, in her father-in-law's house she shall be dignified and modest, inside and out, and shall not cause any person to sin, for because of such transgressions women die in childbirth, or bear destructive children, or their sons and daughters die while young - but those who are careful merit worthy offspring, fit and holy, and shall reach old age, glad and joyful.
Pele Yoetz 5:1: Love of Torah Scholars and Those Who Fear the LORD and Esteem His Name - Love of Torah scholars and those who fear the LORD and esteem His Name is also drawn from love of the Omnipresent, for whoever has a faithful friend loves also his children and his household. And further, since he has intense love with his beloved and seeks his good with all his soul and all his heart, whoever does good and gives peace of mind to his beloved, he loves him. And further, we have already said that intellect requires loving a precious man, complete in attributes and opinions, whoever resembles him being a man of virtue, or loving perfection even if it is not within himself. Behold, from all these reasons they saw fit to arouse love for Torah scholars and for those who fear the LORD and esteem His Name (Malachi 3:16), that they be as beloved as the pupil of one's eye. And behold, his reward is with him, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Shabbat 23b): whoever loves the Sages shall have sons who are Sages. And the essential love is in the heart, but it must also be recognizable in deed - that if the LORD has widened his boundary, he shall support Torah scholars with all his soul and his strength, and shall act with actual deeds; and if his hand does not reach that far, at the very least he shall serve them greatly with his own body, with all his strength, in a manner that, without disturbance, they may stand guard over Torah and over the service of the Name - and great is the deed, as shall be written further below. And needless to say, he must guard his soul greatly not to cause pain to a Torah scholar, and that no Torah scholar find in him a cause for grievance - and the Tanna has already warned (Avot 2:10, Tanchuma Yitro 12): warm yourself before the fire of the Sages, but be careful of their glowing coals lest you be burned, and so on.
Pele Yoetz 5:2: And if the obligation of love for Torah scholars is great even when they are not one's relatives, since all are considered like relatives, all the more so if the Torah scholar is a relative of one's own family, whom one is obligated to love even more and more - and an obligation falls upon his brothers and all his relatives to support him with even greater strength and even greater vigor, that he stand guard over Torah and over the service of the Name. And this shall be for them a praise, a name, and a glory, and through this they honor their father, that he have peace of mind through his son the Torah scholar, and they too shall take their share - each man his share of all his labor which he has labored - and it is found that he does kindness with the dead and with the living. Therefore, happy is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds fast to it (Isaiah 56:2). It is a tree of life to those who hold fast to it, and those who support it are praiseworthy (Proverbs 3:18).
Pele Yoetz 5:3: However, not because a person provides for the needs of a Torah scholar shall he make light of it, God forbid, and not credit himself with the good of feeding and sustaining him, for his own portion is embedded within his own possessions, as they said on the verse (Exodus 22:24), "the poor with you" - meaning, it is the agency of the Merciful One that he performs - and moreover, more than the wealthy does for the poor, the poor does for the wealthy, for through him the wealthy man merits a good name forever, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Ruth Rabbah 5:9, Vayikra Rabbah 34:8) on the verse (Ruth 2:19), "the man with whom I worked today is named Boaz" - therefore he shall be careful of his honor. And Torah scholars, too, must be careful of the honor of their wealthy brothers who benefit them and support them. For if they said (Eruvin 86a) that Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi] and Rabbi Akiva would honor the wealthy even though they did not need anything from them, all the more so one who needs them and benefits from them - an obligation rests upon him not to be ungrateful, but to honor them somewhat and take some trouble on their behalf to give them peace of mind, and let extra affection be known to them, and let them learn from them the way they should walk and the deeds they should do (Exodus 18:20), with pleasant speech and a tongue of affection - "open rebuke is better" (Proverbs 27:5) than [hidden] love - and let them share in their trouble, to grieve for them and pray for them, and let their prayer for them always be that they act wisely in all they do, and in all their Torah and their good deeds let them also have them in mind. And of such and similar matters, let the wise man hear and increase learning (Proverbs 1:5), and let him act in a manner that he find favor and good sense in the eyes of God and man.
Pele Yoetz 6:1: Love of Fellows - It is known how great is the virtue of love of fellows, to the point that our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Yerushalmi Nedarim 9:4), "and you shall love your fellow as yourself" is a great principle of the Torah - and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, explained it (Shabbat 31a) to mean: that which is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. And behold, according to the greatness of the good, so does a person's inclination overpower him every day, to the point that, because of our sins, because of the sin of baseless hatred, our city was destroyed and our Temple laid desolate and we were exiled from our land, and still Satan dances among us to incite us - each man turns to his own gain and does not concern himself with his fellow's stumbling, and there are those who rejoice at calamity, and there are those who, for the sake of any small benefit, swallow their fellow man alive. Woe to the eyes that see such things, for our eyes fail with looking for our expected salvation, and there is no savior as long as this trait is found among us. Therefore one must strengthen himself to arouse love. And the details of love of fellows have already been explained at length in "Sefer HaBrit," and I shall come briefly. And it is that one must fulfill in this matter "turn away from evil and do good" (Psalms 34:15), and one must turn away from evil in speech and in deed.
Pele Yoetz 6:2: In speech - that which is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow. One must be careful and guard against speaking to his fellow or about his fellow any speech that he would not want spoken to him or about him, and this includes gossip, verbal wronging, and many similar things. And so, in this manner, one must turn away from evil.
Pele Yoetz 6:3: In deed - not to harm his fellow or cause him any harm, anything that is not pleasing that they should do to him. And one must go deep into this, for the deceptions of the evil inclination are many. And it is especially necessary to be careful in a place involving monetary loss, for a person is prone to rule leniently for his own benefit and to incline after gain that comes to him even at his fellow's loss. And not for nothing did they say (Eruvin 65b): a person is recognized by his pocket. Happy is the man who fears the LORD and loves the LORD with all his might, and does not incline after gain.
Pele Yoetz 6:4: And so one must fulfill in this mitzvah "and do good" in speech and in deed: in speech - to speak good and proper words to gladden people, such as good tidings and good counsel, and to remove an obstacle from his fellow's path, to inform him if he learns that some harm shall reach him in any way, and to comfort him in his time of trouble, and many similar things. And in deed - to do kindness with body and with money, just as he desires that they do for him and have mercy on him and exert themselves to have mercy on him, so shall he do, in order to perform kindness and fulfill the mitzvah "you shall love your fellow as yourself." Happy is the man who does this, and the son of man who holds fast to it (Isaiah 56:2). Reward is according to the pain (Avot) - for according to the pain, he gives satisfaction to his Former. And like a father's compassion for his children, and a brother born for adversity (Proverbs 17:17), so shall a man help his fellow, for we are all sons of one man (Genesis 42:11), we are brothers. And just as one has mercy on one of his own limbs, so must he have mercy on every person of Israel, for we are all like one man, like one body.
Pele Yoetz 6:5: And behold, a person loves himself and his son and his brother because nature obligates him to, but regarding his fellow, in a place where he thinks there is loss or physical trouble involved, love of self overpowers him - and all the more so, since the matter is a great mitzvah, a person's inclination overpowers him to sway him against his Maker's will, so that he lose much good, and one must overcome his inclination and have mercy on his Maker's honor and arouse love. And happy is Israel - how much toil they endure, how much trouble they bear, and how much expense they lay out for the sake of a mitzvah and good deeds - happy is their portion. But the trouble is that there are great mitzvot which have no advocate, because they are not considered mitzvot to such a degree. And if they said (Avot 4:2), "run to a minor mitzvah as to a major one, for you do not know the reward given for mitzvot," all the more so for such a great mitzvah as this, which includes love of kindness, love of fellows, and the ways of peace, which is worthy of being pursued as one pursues life. And since the inclination nearby teaches forty-nine ways to purify the impure creeping thing and to bring benefit to oneself, and especially since there are, in this matter, several considerations by which one who fears the word of the LORD becomes confused and does not know which way holds the light, therefore the counsel counseled is to fulfill the Tanna's statement, who said (ibid. 4:13[some editions]): do not rely on your own understanding. And this is a great principle in the entire Torah, and all the more so in monetary matters: "he who walks with the wise shall become wise" (Proverbs 13:20) and shall attain the paths of life.
Pele Yoetz 6:6: And the essential mitzvah of love is in the heart - that he not rejoice, God forbid, at his fellow's stumbling, but rather rejoice at his good and be pained at his trouble, to the point of praying for him. And the way to acquire this love is when he takes to heart their saying, of blessed memory (Chagigah 15b), that even at the time when the wicked are in distress, the Shechinah is distressed, [asking] what does the tongue say, and so on. And it follows that when a person is at ease, the Shechinah too is at ease - and if so, a person who loves the LORD should rejoice in the joy of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, and be distressed in their distress. And further, when a person is at ease and has wealth and possessions, he shall not lack for increasing mitzvot and good deeds, giving satisfaction to our Former - which is not so when a person is in distress, for his heart is not with him, and he falls short in the service of the Name, blessed be He, and poverty leaves no room for a good trait, and therefore he transgresses against his Maker's will and grieves the One who bore him.
Pele Yoetz 6:7: And from what has been said, let the wise man hear that one should rejoice greatly when he sees people doing their Maker's will, and grieve in his soul over transgressors. And even if he himself falls short in the service of the Creator, he should not desire that his fellow be like him as well, so that "the trouble of the many" become "a comfort to fools." To what is this comparable? To a noblewoman who has ten sons, and the king commanded them to feed and sustain her and to supply her sufficient needs. And one day, one of the king's sons broke the law and did not give his portion to his mother - although he shall surely be punished, nevertheless the son who loves his mother and is pained at his own failure to give his portion shall ask whether at least his brothers completed their portions, for in this he would find half a comfort. And if they say that they all betrayed her like him, his distress shall grow, for his mother shall weep and wail over having been left in hunger, thirst, and want. And the parable is understood on its own. And further, a person should rejoice in his fellow's good fortune, since with an increase of good he shall increase the performance of mitzvot and good deeds, and through an increase in the performance of mitzvot and good deeds, good reaches him too, that his own debts not tip the scale of the whole world to the side of guilt, so that he be punished for all the evil he causes - and with an increase of good, through his fellow tipping the world to the side of merit, on the day of good he too shall be among the good.
Pele Yoetz 6:8: And behold, King Solomon, peace be upon him, said (Proverbs 10:12): "hatred stirs up strife, but love covers all transgressions." And there are causes over which hatred is stirred between a man and his brother, and it is all vanity and vexation of spirit. There is one who hates because his fellow sinned against him, in his body, his money, or his honor - and for this the Torah has already commanded (Leviticus 19:18): "you shall not take vengeance nor bear a grudge." And they explained the reason: that man was compelled in his deeds, and performed the agency of the Merciful One, for the LORD told him to curse, and his own bad fortune caused the guilt to roll about through him who was liable - and since this is so, there is no place to hate his fellow, for he is like an axe in the hand of the one who hews with it. And why should a living man complain, a man for his sins (Lamentations 3:39)? And there is one who hates out of jealousy, thinking that through his fellow his own livelihood is diminished - and this is nothing but small faith, as we shall explain under the entry "Emunah" [faith], with the help of Heaven. And there is one who hates because he sees that his fellow does not walk in a good way - and for this the living person shall take to heart that he too has faults, even more so according to his own measure, for everything is according to what kind of man he is; a scale and just balances are in the hand of the LORD (Proverbs 16:11). And if his fellow's inclination overpowered him and he transgressed against his Maker's will, while to himself the LORD extended kindness and guided him in the way of truth, should he not give thanks to the LORD and be careful about the fine details of mitzvot to the hair's breadth, according to his own knowledge and understanding and the help of the Almighty that was granted him - rather than disgrace and hate his brother in his heart? For there is no permission to hate except a wicked man who, after being rebuked several times, nevertheless persists in his rebellion and provokes our Father in Heaven, causing pain in Heaven - but toward every other person it is forbidden to hate. And the Tanna already went to great lengths in condemning hatred, to the point of saying (Avot 2:11): hatred of one's fellow creatures removes a person from the world.
Pele Yoetz 6:9: And the great fence to remove hatred is fulfilling the Tanna's statement (ibid. 1:6): judge every person favorably. And even if your own eyes see the curse in one who does wrong, you should not blame him so much and hate him, since "every man's way is right in his own eyes," and what could he have done - "a man does what is right in his own eyes." We have nothing but to pour out our soul before the LORD, that He set us right with good counsel from before Him, and guide us in paths of righteousness for His Name's sake. And if a person says, does not the Holy One, blessed be He, punish a person for walking after the willfulness of his heart and what is right in his own eyes, since he should have learned and did not learn - you too shall say to him: this applies to one who is exacting [with others], for they are exacting with him in turn; but one who overlooks his own attributes [forgoing strict justice], they overlook all his transgressions (Yoma 23a, Megillah 28a), and with the measure a person measures, they measure to him (Megillah 12b, Sotah 8b). But a person should not hate his fellow for not walking in the way of the good, for if so, he should hate himself even more - for who assured his heart to say that he has gone deep and expanded, that he has done everything within his power as he ought to have done it, such that he is not worse than his fellow? And perhaps his fellow is better than him according to his own measure, understanding, and ability - as in the well-known saying of the sage who honored every person, saying: if he is wiser than I, it is fitting to honor him for his wisdom, and if he is a fool compared to me, it is fitting to honor him, for he is better than I, since he sins unwittingly and I sin knowingly. And so, in this manner, of such and similar matters, the living person shall take pure thoughts to heart, to drive away hatred and arouse love. Behold, his reward is with him - he increases a good trait.
Pele Yoetz 6:10: And it is true that our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Bava Metzia 33a): his own lost object and his father's or teacher's lost object - his own takes precedence. But they already said there in the Talmud: whoever always maintains this for himself, in the end comes to this [i.e., poverty]. And Rashi explained that if he is always exacting in this manner to look out for his own benefit, he thereby frees himself from acts of kindness and charity, and in the end he shall need [to be sustained by] others. Rather, he must be willing to lose a little himself so that his fellow not lose, or so that his fellow gain much, or so as to save his fellow from trouble - and through this the LORD shall command a blessing with him.
Pele Yoetz 6:11: And the essential love of fellows is that he clothe himself in his fellow's own person, in a manner that even if his fellow himself is not particular about his own honor and disgrace, nevertheless it should be considered as though, if he himself were like his fellow, according to his own character, he would want to be honored and would not want anyone to speak any wronging words to him or touch his honor - so shall he do to his fellow. This is a general principle in love of fellows, and through this "the LORD shall give strength to His people, the LORD shall bless His people with peace" (Psalms 29:11).
Pele Yoetz 7:1: Mourning - Mourning over the destruction of the Temple is a matter dependent on deed, especially during the period between the Seventeenth of Tammuz and the Ninth of Av, by day and by night: to place ashes where one lays tefillin, to sit near the mezuzah, and to say the order of Tikkun Chatzot [midnight lament]. However, the deed is not the essential thing - rather, one must have an eye weeping bitterly and a broken and crushed heart, sighing like a mourner in gloom with a broken spirit over the distress of Heaven, and all according to one's knowledge, according to the abundance of love, and according to the merit of the soul. And it is true that we have become so impoverished that none among us knows what we have lost, what we have forfeited, and what we have caused through our many sins, nor what the exile of the Shechinah is, nor to what degree Her distress and the distress of the upper and lower worlds reach - over this let all who grieve, grieve. Nevertheless, every person is only obligated according to his own measure, and he shall picture to himself as though his mother were girded in sackcloth, dressed in black and wrapped in black, crying bitterly aloud, moaning like a dove. What does the tongue say (Sanhedrin 46a)? Woe is my head, woe is my arm. "Sons I have raised and exalted, and they have rebelled against Me" (Isaiah 1:2). And of such and similar matters the living person shall take to heart words that embitter the heart, and shall pour out his soul with a voice of wailing - perhaps he shall merit to see the comfort of Zion and the building of our Temple, our glory, may it be built speedily in our days, Amen.
Pele Yoetz 7:2: And from this you shall understand how evil and bitter is the deed that some men or women do, gathering together to rejoice in the joy of frivolous company on Saturday nights and other nights, especially winter nights, increasing in vain merriment, eating and drinking, playing music and singing songs of love and remnants of idolatrous song. Woe to them, alas for them, for without doubt their joy shall be turned to sorrow for them, whether in this world or in the World to Come, if they do not take it to heart to repent - for besides the several prohibitions they commit through a session of scoffers and vulgar speech in songs of love, and our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Sotah 48a): an ear that listens to [such] singing shall be plucked out - moreover, "a foolish son is a grief to his father, and bitterness to her who bore him" (Proverbs 17:25), for the Holy One, blessed be He, shall say: woe, cruel children! A voice is heard on high, wailing, bitter weeping - Rachel weeping for her children (Jeremiah 31:14), and she is like a virgin girded in sackcloth. "And the LORD shall roar from on high, and give forth His voice from His holy dwelling; He shall roar mightily over His habitation." And the angels of peace weep bitterly, and all the heavenly host on high, the righteous, the pious, and our righteous Messiah, weep and lament - all over the destruction of the Temple, destroyed because of our sins - while we, at that very time, sit and sing, glad and joyful in frivolous merriment. This is nothing but evil of heart and blindness of eyes. Whoever fears the LORD and is tender of heart, upon hearing such words, shall take it to heart not to attend such frivolous merriment and optional feasts anymore, but shall remain in sorrow always, rejoicing only in the joy of a mitzvah - and through this "Israel shall rejoice in his Maker."
Pele Yoetz 7:3: And included in the mitzvah of mourning is that when a death occurs for which one is obligated to mourn, he should be careful to fulfill the laws of mourning precisely, as our Rabbis, of blessed memory, established, as detailed in the Shulchan Aruch (Yoreh De'ah 342). And many of the common people do not know to be careful, out of lack of knowledge, and study words of Torah and put on leather shoes and seek to distract their minds from mourning. If only they were wise, they would understand that at a time when the attribute of judgment is stretched taut over him, he must be all the more careful to fulfill everything precisely and accept upon himself the judgment of Heaven - and he shall weep bitterly for three days of weeping, the living man shall lament, each man for his own sins, and all seven days he shall occupy himself with eulogy, telling the praises of the deceased and whatever good was found in him, and he shall study the laws of mourning or difficult matters, in a manner that he not distract his mind from mourning - for they forbade even the conversation of children, so that he not distract his attention. And when he fulfills the words of the Sages, he is assured that he shall not continue to grieve further. And it is fitting for every person, when such a matter befalls him, God forbid, to seek out books on the laws of mourning - and if he does not know the Holy Tongue, let him seek books in the vernacular, such as the Shulchan Aruch in translation and the book "Me'am Lo'ez" on Parashat Vayechi and the like. And this applies to every person, that he seek to know what he should do, as required, from the mouths of scholars or from the mouths of books, and not transgress against his Maker's will - and through this joy shall be in his dwelling.
Pele Yoetz 7:4: And especially for one's father and mother it is fitting to show extra mourning for a full twelve months, and he should not enter into any joyous occasion or any feast, and should not go to visit any person either on Sabbaths or on festivals, and meanwhile he should increase his Torah study for their repose and the elevation of their souls, and should not go on excursions at all, and should always consider: perhaps they are in distress, so how can I be at ease? And a person should not say, what benefit or addition is there in my mourning for them - can I thereby bring them back? Not so, my father - for they said in the Aggadah, brought by the Ramban, of blessed memory, in Torat HaAdam (page 27b), that Moses our teacher, peace be upon him, said to Joshua: Joshua, wear black for me and cover yourself in black, and be careful of the honor of this humbled one - see there. This implies that it is an honor to the soul, whatever mourning is shown over its departure - but he should not do as is the custom in some places, to wear weekday clothes on the Sabbath [of the mourning week]; this should not be done even on the Sabbath that falls within the seven days [of mourning], according to the words of the master Ari, of blessed memory, by whose teaching we live. Let the righteous man hold to his way, the way of holiness, for all his ways are just and his words are life.
Pele Yoetz 8:1: Faith - Faith was made the cornerstone. For whoever believes in the LORD, whose glory fills the whole earth and whose eyes are open upon all the ways of the sons of man, to give each man according to his ways and the fruit of his deeds - "the righteous shall live by his faith" - shall surely be careful to fulfill all the mitzvot and the fine details of the mitzvot, shall be swift in mitzvot and careful to be clean of all sin, shall be strong as a lion in the service of his Creator, and shall not turn back before anyone. For with his eyes he shall see and his heart shall understand that the Name of the LORD is called upon him and His eyes roam over the whole earth - an eye sees, an ear hears, and all his deeds are written in a book. And he shall be ashamed before Him and serve Him a complete service, in fear, love, and great joy, and shall believe with complete faith that there is good reward for the righteous according to the abundance of deeds and according to the pain, the reward - and evil and bitter punishment for the wicked for every transgression. And a scale and just balances are in the hand of the LORD, to give each man according to his ways, according to his measure, his understanding, and his ability, and according to his effort and joy, arrangement corresponding to arrangement.
Pele Yoetz 8:2: And there is another aspect of faith, from which several good virtues are drawn - namely, to believe in His providence, blessed be He, over the lower worlds in every single detail, and that a person does not so much as stub his finger below unless it is decreed upon him from above (Chullin 7b), and that from the Most High goes forth both evil and good, whether coming by the hand of Heaven or by the hand of man - for the Omnipresent has many agents, both for good and for less good, and He is the One who gives the power to do valiantly (Deuteronomy 8:18), for bread does not come to the wise, nor the race to the swift (Ecclesiastes 9:11). And because of this, he shall not spare his money's loss in a place involving the service of his Maker, to do His will, nor shall he labor to grow rich through forbidden means, but rather shall conduct his affairs justly and properly, according to the Torah, and shall not be exacting, nor flatter, nor hate his brother, nor take vengeance, nor bear a grudge - for he knows and believes that the LORD told him to curse, and everything comes from Him to correct his own crookedness for his own good. "A God of faith without iniquity, just and upright is He" (Deuteronomy 32:4). "The LORD is righteous in all His ways and pious in all His deeds" (Psalms 145:17). And whatever the Merciful One does, He does for the good (Berachot 60b). And through this he shall accept the judgment of Heaven with joy, and shall not be repelled by His rebuke.
Pele Yoetz 8:3: And the root of everything is to believe in all the words of the Torah and in all the words of the Sages, and if his own mind cannot bear it, let him attribute it to his own lack of knowledge and limited understanding - but let him believe with complete faith that all their words are living and enduring and faithful forever and for all eternity. Come and see how great are the words of the Sages, who said that the entire Torah is included and hidden within the attribute of faith. And many say with their mouths that they are believers, sons of believers, but their deeds differ, and deed comes and removes what was said by word. And for all this, God shall bring into judgment those who walked in darkness - besides the punishment for the transgression itself, he shall be further punished for lacking faith. Or if he believes and nevertheless does not care to walk in the proper way, this is brazenness and the forehead of a harlot.
Pele Yoetz 8:4: And behold, these mitzvot too - to believe in the existence of the LORD and to believe in His providence - are among the 613 mitzvot, and they are constant mitzvot which one can fulfill at every time and every moment through remembrance alone. Behold, it is thus good for a man to remember with his mouth and not forget in his heart, and time and again the Israelite servant shall say: what do you want of me, my inclination, always pursuing me? The LORD shall rebuke you, Satan, for I am a Jew, son of a Jew, and I believe with complete faith in the existence of the LORD always before me and in His particular providence over every single detail, and that He repays a good reward for every good thing - thought, speech, and deed - and an evil and bitter punishment for every evil thing, even for idle chatter and every evil thought. Behold, it is therefore fitting for me to do thus and so, and to conduct myself in this way and in this manner, and to withdraw my hand and be careful and guard against this and that, until my deeds be pure and upright in thought, speech, and deed, with no crookedness or perversity found in them, so that my faith not be false - so shall I do and not change. And of such and similar matters, the living person shall take it to heart, and shall persist in his thought and go deep into it in its length and breadth, to walk in the paths of faith, and his hands shall be faithfulness - hands that prove that he was faithful. Then good is faithfulness, to merit the life of the World to Come, a true rest - and the essential thing in all of it is to give satisfaction before the One who dwells on high.
Pele Yoetz 9:1: Eating and Drinking - Eating and drinking have three categories: mitzvah, permitted, and forbidden. And it is within a person's power to make all his meals meals of mitzvah, by combining these conditions truly stated by the mouths of scholars, by whose teaching we live. First, he must intend in his eating to be healthy and strong for the service of God, blessed be His Name, and to be "one who deals kindly with his own soul" (Proverbs 11:17) - namely, to clarify and bring to light all the sparks of holiness attached to everything he eats and drinks. And he must pray for his sustenance before every meal, and this is a great obligation, as explained in the Zohar (Shemot, page 62). (And I, the lowly one, have arranged a text of prayer to express in words the intentions we have mentioned, for there is benefit in verbal expression for the heart's remembrance, and it shall also help draw holiness upon the eating, especially since his intention is for the sake of Heaven, and I have appended it to my "Beit Tefillati" [House of My Prayer], with the help of Heaven.) And behold, whoever reads in the holy book "Reshit Chokhmah" (Gate of Holiness, ch. 15) shall see with his own eyes the intentions for eating, which correspond in their measures to the sacrifices. Happy is the one born of woman whose hand can reach to build his chambers in heaven through his own eating, provided he directs his heart to Heaven and does the matter according to law and precept - and "clean hands add strength" (Job 17:9) to be careful with the washing of hands properly and as the Sages established.
Pele Yoetz 9:2: And he shall clothe himself in trembling when he comes to bless his Maker, who prepared his food and his other pleasures - how very much must he be careful to say the blessings precisely, letter by letter, word by word, and especially in mentioning the Name of the LORD, all his bones shall shudder with trembling - for to the King, the LORD of hosts, high and exalted, he lifts up a blessing, and if he is not careful, God forbid, he blasphemes the LORD, and afterward comes the heart's intention - these are the essentials. Therefore one must be careful with all the blessings, and especially with the blessing over enjoyment, and even more so with Grace after Meals, which is of Torah origin - not because it is long shall it be rushed, but rather arranged according to law and precept, and this is a matter that reason itself obligates and the eye sees in the way of the world, even regarding a blessing to an ordinary person - all the more so and how much more so when coming to bless the King of glory, awesome and fearsome, who in His great kindness permitted us to bless Him and mention His honored and awesome Name, which is counted as a mitzvah for us, and He establishes for us reward and blessing for the blessing - therefore one must be careful to say it according to law. And a fence for this is to say all the blessings aloud, for the voice arouses intention, and he shall know for certain whether he has blessed, and shall not enter into doubt, and shall merit and cause others to answer Amen after him, and they shall learn from him if they are not expert. And one must also be careful to fulfill the words of our Sages, of blessed memory, to dip the slice of the Hamotzi bread in salt three times, and not to omit this where possible, for all their words stand at the summit of the world.
Pele Yoetz 9:3: And one must sit with dignity at the table, for he eats at the King's table. And the well-known deed of the master Rabbi Yisrael Nagara, in the time of the Ari, of blessed memory, is known - that he would sing at his table in a pleasant voice, and the ministering angels would gather as at the wedding celebrations of bride and groom, and his arms were exposed because of the heat, and a voice from Heaven fell: flee from this man, who diminishes the honor of Heaven, for he does not sit with dignity at the table which is before the LORD - and immediately they all flew away. And the master Ari would see from his house this great vision, and revealed his secret to the master Rabbi Yisrael Nagara, who trembled a great trembling, adorned himself, and sat with dignity, and resumed singing as before, and the ministering angels returned to gather as at first. Therefore, whoever fears the word of the LORD shall speak entirely of honor. And one must be careful to eat in a civilized manner, and not like the gluttonous and greedy, of whom it is said in the Holy Zohar (Vayechi, page 246) that they are from the side of Esau, of whom it is written (Genesis 25:30), "let me gulp down," and he is despised and loathsome in the eyes of God and man.
Pele Yoetz 9:4: And one must also be careful to eat to satisfy his soul, and not fill his belly to distend it with gross eating, for "there wickedness has settled" - all who go about with a distended belly aim toward the evil inclination, for so the Kabbalists have written, that whatever a person adds on a weekday beyond what suffices for satiety adds strength to the Other Side and strengthens his own evil inclination, that it overpower him - and all the more so, one who increases optional feasts and frivolous merriment adds great strength to the Other Side, for just as a mitzvah is elevated and adds strength to the heavenly retinue when performed by many together, so too correspondingly, a transgression performed by many is indeed multiplied and adds strength to the Other Side. And the sages of ethics have already written that one who eats more than he needs does several bad things: first, he transgresses "do not destroy"; and further, he wastes the time of eating and the time of relieving himself; and if his stomach becomes upset and he is troubled, that makes three [wasted] times; and if he becomes ill and dies, he is liable for his own life. Therefore, one who guards his soul shall distance himself from excessive eating and drinking - he shall eat only when hungry, and shall not eat until he is completely full, but rather somewhat less. And the Ra'avad wrote that one who withholds his hand from food pleasant to his palate, for the atonement of his sins, is considered as though he had fasted and as an altar of atonement (Rabbeinu Yonah, in the book Yesod HaTeshuvah). And behold, this is the clever one - he eats to satisfy his soul and it is considered as though he had fasted. And one who eats for the sake of Heaven shall not pursue what is pleasant to the palate and harmful to the body, but rather what is beneficial to the body, even if it is not so pleasant to his palate. And he must be especially careful about excessive drinking, for it is a fire that consumes unto destruction, and mighty are all its slain. Many have drunk - a demon they have drunk - devastation and ruin within their borders, evil for them and evil for the world. And our Sages, of blessed memory, have already gone to great lengths in condemning them. And especially for a Torah scholar, the pain is great if he drinks and steps out of line among the common people, for the Name of Heaven is desecrated through him. And happy is the discerning man who conducts his affairs with judgment.
Pele Yoetz 9:5: It is written (Proverbs 23:2): "and put a knife to your throat if you are a man given to appetite." How very much must one be careful of every hint of prohibition that depends on eating, for one thereby increases the transgression and the guilt of that soul - it goes from evil to evil, for its impurity is in its skirts, and it shall not be able to attain the paths of life, to fear and to love the honored and awesome LORD and to serve Him a complete service. Therefore one must be careful and vigilant, and stand over the ritual slaughterers, that they be skilled craftsmen and God-fearing men, well recognized; and he shall urge the members of his household to check very well, as far as their hand can reach, against the prohibition of insects, and shall not eat fruit in which worms grow until he first cuts it open and checks it - and likewise one must be very careful of mosquitoes and fleas and various tiny creeping creatures that fall into food in the summer months, even unknowingly, and must be expert in the laws of wines and foods regarding contact with idolaters and what is hidden from the eye, and the like. And how good and how pleasant it is to conduct oneself with abstinence and to flee a hundred gates of the permitted so as not to enter one gate of the forbidden, for all of a man's labor is for his mouth (Ecclesiastes 6:7), and "he who guards his mouth and his tongue guards his soul from troubles" (Proverbs 21:23).
Pele Yoetz 9:6: And one must be careful not to be exacting with the members of his household about anything, and this includes the matter of eating - even if she scorched his dish and did not prepare what would suit him, and he should not treat an unwitting act as intentional, nor an act done under duress as one done willingly. And he shall not be angry with his wife, his servants, and the members of his household, for a person is judged from Heaven measure for measure, and it is written (Job 31:13-14): "if I despised the cause of my manservant or my maidservant when they contended with me, what then shall I do when God rises up? And when He visits, what shall I answer Him?" Go deep into this and overlook your own attributes, for more than your wife and your servants are obligated in your honor and your service, you are obligated in the honor and service of your Maker.
Pele Yoetz 9:7: And one must be careful to say words of Torah at the table, and not let a verse of Scripture or a Mishnah pass by unmentioned. And when he is in the company of people, if he is capable, his mouth shall utter wisdom, to merit himself and others with him; and if he is not capable, or if the matter is not readily available to him, at the very least he shall study to himself some Mishnah that is fluent on his lips, such as "Kol Yisrael" or "Rabbi Chananya," and the like, and whoever increases this is praiseworthy. And since the Holy Zohar (Shemot, page 157b) went to great lengths regarding the praise that reaches above through remembering the Temple at one's table and being distressed and worried over its absence, I have therefore made it a practice to say this baraita at the table, to also fulfill thereby the obligation of words of Torah: It is taught: Rabbi Yose said: once I was walking on the road and I entered one of the ruins of Jerusalem to pray, and so on (Berachot 3a). It is taught: Rabbi Elazar says: the night has three watches, and so on (ibid.). Yehudah ben Teima says, and so on (Avot 5:20). And on the Sabbath I am accustomed to say the teaching of Yehudah ben Teima, and from there, "Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Yose: whoever delights in the Sabbath is given an inheritance without bounds," and so on (Shabbat 118a). "Rabbi Chananya ben Akashya," and so on. And afterward, the heart's intentions are the essentials - in a time of sorrow, sorrow; and in a time of joy, joy.
Pele Yoetz 9:8: And the man whose boundary the LORD has widened - how pleasant is his lot if he is careful to give a portion of his meal to the poor man who lacks it, for "a man's gift makes room for him" (Proverbs 18:16) in this world and in the World to Come. And how good it is to raise an orphan boy or girl within his household, for through this his righteousness stands forever at every single meal. And one whose hand is limited shall intend to fulfill this when he feeds his own sons and daughters, for this too is called performing charity at all times. And on the Sabbath and festivals, it is proper for every man to sing at his table, giving voice to honor his Maker for the grace He has graced us with.
Pele Yoetz 9:9: Mayim Acharonim [the final ritual hand-washing after a meal] is an obligation, at home and away, on the Sabbath and on weekdays. And many have overstepped and abolished this washing, especially travelers. And one must be even more careful about it than about the first washing [before the meal] - and whoever transgresses the words of the Sages is liable for death (Berachot 4b), and reward is according to the pain.
Pele Yoetz 9:10: And at a mitzvah feast, one must be careful that its reward not be lost through its loss, through something improper such as mockery, slanderous talk, wronging speech, laughter and levity, and the like - rather, the fear of Heaven shall always cover him, and through this his eating shall be accepted like a fire-offering, and when he conducts himself properly according to the Torah, his table shall be an altar of atonement.
Pele Yoetz 9:11: And one must recite Grace after Meals calmly, aloud, and with a joyful heart. For if he takes to heart the words that come out of his mouth, to intend them deeply, it is impossible not to rejoice. And as appears from the words of the Holy Zohar (Shemot, page 208[?]), there is a great need and personal obligation to do everything possible in order to recite Grace after Meals with joy. And the great fence for intending properly is to bless with closed eyes, or with his eyes lowered and his heart raised. And he shall intend, in the four blessings, the four letters of the Name, to draw forth abundance and blessing into the four worlds: Atzilut, Beriah, Yetzirah, Asiyah. Happy is the one born of woman who merits this! And the Chinuch wrote (mitzvah 430) that there is a tradition that whoever is careful with Grace after Meals, his sustenance is assured to him with honor all the days of his life. Go forth and learn from the reward of giving great satisfaction to his Former, and let all your deeds be for the sake of Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 10:1: Truth - "A lip of truth shall be established forever" (Proverbs 12:19), and it saves from death, as known from the Talmud's statement (Sanhedrin 97a) about that place called Kushta [Truth], where they did not speak falsehood, and no man died before his time. And our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (ibid. 92a) that whoever changes his word is considered as one who worships idols, as it is written (Genesis 27:12), "and I shall be in his eyes as a mocker." And the LORD God is truth, His seal is truth (Shabbat 55a), and His Torah is truth, and the remnant of Israel shall not do injustice nor speak falsehood, nor shall a deceitful tongue be found in their mouth (Zephaniah 3:13). And there are many of the common people whose tongue has learned to speak falsehood, and it has become for them like something fully permitted, to the point that some lie in vain, idle stories, without any benefit, of whom Scripture says (Isaiah 5:18): "woe to those who draw iniquity with cords of vanity." And when it is done to attain some benefit, such as in weights and measures and the like, then it is not called by the name falsehood, but by the name shrewdness, sharpness, and diligence, and they say that whoever does not lie in this age cannot earn a living. And they have answered falsely, for our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said in Midrash Mishlei (Midrash Tehillim 7:11, and see Yalkut Shimoni Shemot remez 56 and Tehillim remez 638): when Noah entered the ark, Falsehood too came to enter. He [Noah] said to him, go and find yourself a mate, for all who come to the ark come male and female. He went and searched and found Loss [Pechata]. He said to her, would you like to be joined with me? She said to him, what will you give me? He answered her, whatever I gain, I shall give to you. And from then on, whatever Falsehood profits, Loss takes for herself. And if the evil inclination has smoothly deceived his eyes and shows him that he profits much through falsehood, in the end, without doubt, loss shall come upon him, as it is written in the words of tradition (Jeremiah 17:11): "he who makes wealth unjustly shall leave it in the midst of his days." And in his end he shall be a base fool, or the wealth shall be kept by its owner to his own harm, in this world and in the World to Come. But the LORD shall not withhold good from those who walk in innocence.
Pele Yoetz 10:2: And the evil of falsehood is evil in the eyes of God and man, for once he is known as a liar, he is despised and loathsome, and the disgrace of the matter is evident to all, to the point that even among the nations of the world there are those who are very careful about the truth of their words and not to speak falsehood. And those who speak falsehood in business dealings with gentiles cause a desecration of God's Name, for the gentiles say: it is known that a Jew is a liar, a deceiver, a wrongdoer, and they speak such evil things about them and cast a blemish upon holy things. And the severity of the prohibition of desecrating God's Name is known, and how many prohibitions are dragged along from falsehood, according to the matter, as the observer shall see. And such is the punishment of the habitual liar - that even when he speaks the truth, no one listens to him.
Pele Yoetz 10:3: And truth is the foundation of the structure. And it is known what they told in the Midrash (Otzar HaMidrashim, page 2299) about a certain man who was utterly wicked, and through accepting upon himself not to speak falsehood, he returned in repentance. For if he went to commit a transgression, he would think: if they ask me [about it], what shall I answer - if I speak the truth I shall be ashamed and humiliated, and if I speak falsehood I shall transgress what I have accepted upon myself. And through this he was restrained and did not walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor did he stand in the way of sinners. And according to the greatness of the virtue of truth and the great disgrace of falsehood and the evils that follow from it, it is fitting for a person to strengthen himself to educate his children in the trait of truth, and from him they shall see that he is exacting about truthfulness and shall do likewise, and he shall stand guard over them so that no deceitful tongue be found in their mouth - and if they do something improper, he shall get them to admit the truth, and thereby they shall be forgiven that time and he shall not strike them, but only urge them not to continue doing it; but if they speak falsehood, he shall add a great blow for the falsehood, and the sin of falsehood shall grow great in their eyes, in a manner that the children shall tremble and be very careful, until it becomes for them a nature not to speak falsehood.
Pele Yoetz 10:4: And included in the trait of truth is to make his words true, whether affirmative or negative, for besides the prohibition involved, it is a disgrace to go back on one's word. And they said (Bava Metzia 44a): He who exacted punishment from the generation of the Flood and the generation of the Dispersion is destined to exact punishment from whoever does not stand by his word. Therefore, one should consider carefully before uttering a word from his mouth whether he can fulfill it, and if he has uttered a word from his mouth, "that which has gone out of your lips you shall keep" (Deuteronomy 23:24), as though he had sworn an oath.
Pele Yoetz 10:5: And since our holy Torah is a Torah of truth, how very much must one be careful to study it in truth, and to admit the truth and accept the truth from whoever says it, even the least of the least. And they have already said: the acknowledgment [in disputes] by the Rabbis is itself their praise. And one should not turn to ways of falsehood through vain and misleading dealings, but rather truth alone shall guide his way - this is the straight path for every upright man who walks in it, and through this he shall find favor and good sense in the eyes of God and man. And more shall be written of this further below, under the entries "Hoda'ah" [acknowledgment] and "Sheker" [falsehood] and the like, for such is our way, to return to a subject.
Pele Yoetz 11:1: Firmness of Heart - Firmness of heart is a great necessity for the service of God, blessed be His Name, for there are many things a person transgresses against his Maker's will because of softness of heart and because of [misplaced] compassion. "A good man conducts his affairs with judgment" (Psalms 112:5), according to the Torah, and shall not deviate, right or left (Deuteronomy 17:11), from what the Torah commanded and what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, commanded - for a person sees in his fellow something improper, and out of concern for his fellow's honor and the like, he places a hand over his mouth [and says nothing]; and likewise sometimes he is concerned about losing his own benefit and flatters - over this and the like, let all who grieve, grieve. And it is likewise known what our Rabbis, of blessed memory, said (Proverbs 12:10): the mercy of the wicked is cruelty. And they said (Eruvin 21b-22a) on the verse (Song of Songs 5:11), "black as a raven" - you find words of Torah only in one who blackens his face over them like a raven, and in one who makes himself cruel toward his sons and the members of his household like a raven. And it is written (Proverbs 23:13-14): "do not withhold discipline from a youth; if you strike him with the rod, he shall not die - you shall strike him with the rod and save his soul from Sheol." And the masters of ethics have already written that women who show excessive affection toward children and prevent their father from striking them - of them Scripture says (Lamentations 4:10), "the hands of compassionate women have cooked their own children" - for she causes it that in the end he shall inherit Gehinnom. Therefore, the wise man's eyes are in his head, and his heart is mighty as the mighty, to keep and fulfill the words of Torah and the words of the Sages as the law requires. And whoever does this is among the disciples of Abraham our father, who, although he was the merciful father, included in the attribute of kindness, made himself cruel toward his only son, born to him in his old age, and "took the knife to slay his son" (Genesis 22:10) to do his Maker's will - and compared to the killing of his son, or the sacrifice of his own life, everything else is light in the scale, and he did not turn back before anyone. Let him take this to heart, to withdraw his hand from doing any evil and to fulfill every good thing - and this applies to every person.
